youtube.title: How Noise-Cancelling Headphones Work (Sound That Erases Sound)
youtube.summary: Noise-cancelling headphones do not just block sound, they fight it with more sound. In this video we see how microphones and a flipped anti-noise wave cancel engine hum, why it works far better on low steady sounds than on voices, how padding handles the rest, and how a frustrated engineer on a flight helped start it all.
youtube.details:
Key facts (checked November 2026):
- ANC uses a microphone and an out-of-phase wave to cancel noise by destructive interference; works best on constant low-frequency sound, less on voices and sudden sounds; high frequencies are handled by passive isolation (Wikipedia: Noise-cancelling headphones)
- Feedforward (outside mic), feedback (inside mic) and hybrid designs (Wikipedia)
- History: Paul Lueg patent 1936; Amar Bose's idea on a flight in 1978; Rutan and Yeager wore prototype Bose headsets on the 1986 non-stop round-the-world flight; Bose consumer QuietComfort from 2000 (Wikipedia)
- Some people feel dizziness with strong ANC; lowering ANC strength can help (SoundGuys)
- Wavelengths calculated with the speed of sound at about 343 m/s

scenes.badge: The anti-noise wave is flipped by
scenes.sub: so it cancels the noise instead of adding to it
scenes.text: You put on a pair of noise cancelling headphones on a plane, press a button, and the roar of the engines almost disappears. It feels like someone turned the world down. But here is the strange part. The headphones do not just block that sound with thicker padding. They fight it by making more sound. They create a copy of the noise that is flipped one hundred and eighty degrees, so that the two cancel each other out. In this video we will see how sound can erase sound, why it works so well on engines but not on voices, and how a frustrated engineer on a flight helped start it all.

scenes.chapterTitle: Push and pull at the same time

items.text: Noise pushes the air forward
Anti-noise pulls it back at the same moment
The air barely moves: silence

scenes.text: Here is a simple way to picture it. Sound is just air being pushed and pulled very quickly. Imagine someone gently pushing a swing forward, while another person pulls it back with exactly the same strength at exactly the same moment. The swing barely moves. Sound waves can do the same thing. If a noise pushes the air forward, and a second sound pulls it back at the same moment, the air near your ear hardly moves at all. And if the air does not move, there is nothing for your ear to hear. That is silence. Sound plus its exact opposite adds up to quiet. Scientists call this destructive interference.

Let us zoom in on what sound actually is. When a speaker or an engine vibrates, it squeezes the air together, then lets it stretch apart, over and over. The squeezed parts are the peaks of the wave, and the stretched parts are the troughs. How many waves pass every second is the frequency, measured in hertz. A deep engine hum might be around a hundred hertz. A high whistle can be thousands. And the distance between two peaks is called the wavelength. To cancel a sound, headphones need to create a wave that puts its peaks exactly where the noise has its troughs, and its troughs where the noise has its peaks.

items.text: A microphone hears the outside noise
The electronics flip the wave upside down
The speaker plays it with your music
A mic inside checks what's left

footer.text: The noise keeps changing, so it never stops

scenes.text: So how do headphones actually do it? First, a tiny microphone on the outside of the ear cup listens to the noise around you. Next, the electronics take that sound and create a wave that is its mirror image. It flips the wave upside down, so every peak becomes a trough. Then the same speaker that plays your music also plays this anti noise, mixed in with your song. Many headphones also have a second microphone inside the ear cup, close to your ear. It listens to what is left over and corrects any mistakes. The noise keeps changing, so the system never stops adjusting.

items.title: Feedforward
items.sub: hears noise before it reaches you

scenes.text: Engineers have names for these setups. A microphone on the outside is called feedforward. It hears the noise before it reaches you, which gives the system a head start. A microphone inside the ear cup is called feedback. It hears exactly what is reaching your ear, so it can catch what the outside microphone missed. Many of today's better headphones use both at once, a design called hybrid. Combining the two lets them cancel noise across a wider range of sounds. That is one reason two pairs of headphones that both say noise cancelling on the box can sound very different in real life.

So why does it work so well on engines, but not on a crying baby? It comes down to wavelength. Sound travels at about three hundred and forty metres per second, so a one hundred hertz hum has waves about three point four metres long. A small timing error barely matters. At a thousand hertz, the wave is only about thirty four centimetres. At ten thousand hertz, it is a tiny three point four centimetres, and the anti noise would have to line up almost perfectly right at your eardrum. Long, steady waves are easy to match. Short, sudden ones are not. That is why the low rumble vanishes, but the higher sounds still get through.

scenes.chapterTitle: What it can and can't cancel
scenes.text: There is a second reason. The headphones are always reacting to sound that has already arrived. A steady noise, like an engine hum or an air conditioning drone, sounds almost the same from one moment to the next, so it is easy to predict and cancel. Voices are different. They change pitch and volume constantly, and they contain lots of higher frequencies. So noise cancelling can soften voices, but it usually cannot erase them. And a sudden sound, like a clap, a bang or breaking glass, is over before the system can respond. Predictable noise is the easiest to erase. That is why a plane cabin is the perfect place for these headphones.

items.text: Ear cups and cushions block high sounds
Ear tips seal the ear canal
The electronics handle the low rumble

scenes.text: So what handles the high sounds? The old fashioned way: physical blocking, called passive isolation. Thick ear cups and soft cushions stop a lot of high pitched sound, because short waves are easily absorbed by padding. In earbuds, a silicone or foam tip seals your ear canal and does the same job. That is why a good fit matters so much. If the seal leaks, both the blocking and the cancelling get worse. So noise cancelling headphones really use two systems working together. Padding takes care of the hiss and chatter, and the electronics take care of the low rumble that padding cannot stop.

scenes.chapterTitle: From a patent to a plane seat

items.text: 1936: Paul Lueg patents the idea
1978: Amar Bose on a noisy flight
1986: headsets on a round-the-world flight
2000: noise cancelling for everyone

scenes.text: The idea is older than you might think. In nineteen thirty six, a German physicist named Paul Lueg patented the basic idea of cancelling sound with sound. But the electronics of the time were not good enough. In nineteen seventy eight, Amar Bose, an engineer and professor at M I T, was on a flight and found that the airline headphones could not beat the engine noise. He started sketching a solution. In nineteen eighty six, pilots Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager wore prototype Bose noise cancelling headsets on their record non stop flight around the world. By two thousand, Bose was selling noise cancelling headphones to everyone, not just pilots.

items.text: Transparency: mics play the world back in
Adaptive modes change the strength
Feel dizzy? Lower the strength

scenes.text: Those same microphones can also do the opposite job. In transparency or ambient mode, the headphones play the outside world back into your ears on purpose, so you can hear traffic or an announcement without taking them off. Many newer models also offer adaptive modes that change the strength of cancelling depending on where you are. One more thing. A small number of people feel slightly dizzy or uneasy with strong noise cancelling. If that happens to you, try to lower the strength in the companion app. It does not mean the headphones are broken, and for most people it is not a problem at all.

items.text: A mic hears the noise, a flipped copy is made
Peaks meet troughs and cancel out
Best on low, steady sounds; padding does the rest

scenes.text: Let us recap in three points. One. A microphone listens to the noise around you, and the electronics create a flipped copy of it. Two. When that anti noise plays, its peaks meet the noise's troughs, and the two cancel out. Three. It works best on low, steady sounds like engines, while padding and a good seal block the higher sounds. The quiet you hear is, quite literally, silence made from sound.

scenes.text: So the next time a plane engine fades away when you press that button, remember that your headphones are not just blocking the noise. They are fighting it with its own mirror image. Now I want to hear from you. Where do you use noise cancelling the most? Tell me in the comments. If you enjoyed this, subscribe to Tech Explained. In the next video, we will go inside a data center, one of the giant buildings that hold the internet.
